item.title: Wan 3.0: Alibaba Moves AI Video from "Short Clip" Mode to "Complete Scene" Mode
item.description:
30 seconds in a single pass, native audio, multiple characters — and even DOC, PDF, PowerPoint, or a web page on input.

Alibaba has opened the preview of Wan 3.0, and this is noticeably more like an attempt to assemble a complete scene from various source materials, rather than just "animating a picture."

I've thoroughly analyzed the features and pricing of the new model, watched the official demos, and compared it to Seedance 2.5 and 2.0, Kling 3.0, MiniMax H3, Veo 3.1, and Grok Imagine.

Inside the article as well — the videos themselves: a 30-second one-take, a cat fighting a snow leopard, eight languages in one song, document-to-video, UGC, and other examples.

Many can already produce five beautiful seconds today. The next benchmark is to get 20–30 seconds of a truly controllable scene: with the same characters, the same objects, proper audio, plot development, and without everything falling apart along the way.

Wan 3.0 is another very significant step in exactly that direction.

Read more

item.title: How agentic AI changes the role of humans in supply chains
item.description:
In a large company, processing a customer order can take up to two hours. Most of this time is spent not on the actions themselves, but on the pauses between them: waiting for a response, double-checking data, approvals.

Agentic orchestration reduces this cycle to a couple of minutes. The agent itself checks inventory, coordinates with logistics, and initiates shipment, while the employee sets rules and evaluates the result, but does not participate in every step.

But if it is so beneficial and produces such an effect, why have most companies not yet implemented and scaled agentic AI? And what is slowing down already launched pilots? These questions were discussed in the McKinsey Talks Operations podcast. The hosts tried to understand why supply chain management, which for decades seemed like one of the most technology-driven tasks, is still stalling in AI adoption.

item.title: CheckMateDB at RSKhB: how we automate automated tests in Java (and why it doesn't replace automation engineers)
item.description:
My name is Mikhail Gerasimov, I am a Chief Engineer at Rosselkhozbank (RSHB), working on the test automation team. Our main focus is regression automated tests in Java.

This publication is the first in a series of articles about CheckMateDB. Here, we will provide a quick but technically substantive overview of the product: what already works, what tasks it addresses, and where we are developing it. In subsequent articles, we will examine individual parts in more detail: module architecture, the ML code generation pipeline, implementation practices, and quality metrics.

In short, our daily reality looks like this: manual testers write scenarios in TestIT, and automation engineers convert them into code. It sounds simple, but at the scale of regression, a bottleneck quickly emerges: between a test case and a finished automated test lies a large layer of repetitive engineering routine. Somewhere you need to carefully collect test data, somewhere write Criteria, somewhere build a PageHelper chain, somewhere finalize checks and stabilize execution. And yes, sometimes it feels like half the automated test has already been written… just in 17 different places and at different times.

In this article, I will tell how our team bridges this gap using CheckMateDB and why we are developing it as a single entry point for automated testing: from data and SQL analytics to AI code generation and controlled change application.

item.title: From subscription to corporate AI: how we built a team of AI developers and overcame employee skepticism
item.description:
For those visiting the blog for the first time: here I talked about AI-ready infrastructure, and here — about its hardware engineering foundation. After the article on information security, it's logical to move from the topic of assembling a technical solution to the topic of "assembling a team" that can implement that solution.

In short, we're talking about local infrastructure for AI in a stack with reality: what it is, why it's needed, and how to actually implement it in the current conditions of the AI market in Russia.

The idea of AI-ready came from personal experience using ChatGPT and a pilot implementation of the model into my company's business processes. A year ago, we didn't have an AI team — just AI enthusiasm. Like many others, we naively assumed we could launch an AI assistant with our existing IT team. After all, even a child can figure out ChatGPT, and a corporate service is only slightly more complex, right?

Wrong. I dedicate this article to all managers who are indiscriminately trying to implement AI into every process today, and to those who think AI can easily replace a hundred employees. Believe me, to create your own working AI tool, you'll need to work three times harder, and finding people who can structure that work properly won't be easy. Just as it's not easy to convince neuro-skeptics and teach a team to fight routine with AI.

Read more

item.title: RAG in medical analytics: how to build a controlled loop instead of yet another chatbot
item.description:
A healthcare organization simultaneously works with electronic medical records, test results, physician reports, clinical guidelines, internal regulations, reporting, and analytical dashboards. The problem lies not only in the volume of information. This data has different structures, is updated at different rates, and is accessible to different user groups.

A BI system effectively displays a metric and its change over time, but it usually does not answer questions about which documents are associated with a deviation, what happened to a specific process, or which sources support the explanation. A large language model can formulate a coherent response, but without a controlled context, it may use outdated information, mix facts with plausible assumptions.

This is where RAG, or Retrieval-Augmented Generation, comes in. However, in a medical environment, I would consider it not as a chatbot and certainly not as an autonomous medical advisor. A more useful model is a controlled layer between data, documents, analytical systems, and users.

item.title: [Translation] OpenAI Jalapeño: OpenAI's personal chip that surpassed NVIDIA Blackwell.
item.description:
OpenAI is creating its own chip, Jalapeño: the end of Nvidia's monopoly on inference?

SemiAnalysis has published an analysis of OpenAI's in-house hardware development, codenamed Jalapeño. While everyone was discussing the procurement of thousands of Nvidia Blackwell GPUs, Sam Altman's team, together with Broadcom, was secretly designing a specialized ASIC on the TSMC N3P process node, tailored exclusively for inference on models of the GPT-4.5 and GPT-5 scale.

item.title: The competition froze on August 16, but the table moved on. I'm figuring out which of this is real.
item.description:
I looked into the data of the Pokemon TCG AI Battle competition to see who was winning, and got stuck on another thing. The public leaderboard shows 6806 teams. The latest solution submission was dated August 16, 23:58:53. After that second, no one submitted.

1668 out of 6806 teams, almost a quarter of the field, made their final submission on that very day: 824 of them after six in the evening, 350 in the last hour. It seems that a considerable number learned about the deadline on the same day it expired.

item.title: IT project passport with the help of AI: a working seven-step framework
item.description:

item.title: AI workstation for investigator
item.description:
You might be interested in how DeepSeek 70B performs on a laptop, but more on that at the end.

I’ll leave aside the reasons for my questioning as a witness—this is, after all, a technical article. That’s where I first saw just how complex working with case materials really is. From the outside, it seems simple: ask questions, record answers, file papers. In reality, you’re faced with testimonies from multiple people, protocols, dates, addresses, phone numbers, photographs, audio recordings, and results of inspections and expert analyses. The materials don’t come in order; some details clarify others, and sometimes they directly contradict each other.

It’s not just about reading all of this. You need to notice that the same person gives different times in two documents, cross-reference statements with phone data, find a recurring VIN or number, reconstruct the sequence of events—and for every conclusion, keep track of the original source. It’s not that law enforcement agencies today still use paper and pen. All case volumes are numbered in pencil, then manually stitched together with a hole punch, just as they were nearly 100 years ago.

And it hit me: this is a job for AI. Zheglov solved cases using card files and intuition. I decided to digitize the card file and replace the intuition with hybrid search—which, unlike Gleb Yegorych, doesn’t fit into 16 GB of VRAM.

item.title: This artificial artificial artificial intelligence
item.description:
In the early 1780s, wealthy Parisians sent their laundry to be washed across the Atlantic in Haiti. The reason was that, aside from the high cost of local services, French laundry after washing would frankly turn yellow, whereas laundry brought back from Saint-Domingue—where the equatorial sun, combined with local indigo, produced a bluish whiteness unattainable in Europe—instead attracted attention and signaled the owner's status.

It's amusing how the scheme of outsourcing to exotic countries still works today: text annotation for popular LLMs is outsourced to cheap labor from, say, Nigeria. But since cheap labor is usually also cunning, manual text annotation services like "Mechanical Turk" have faced the issue that 30% to 50% of workers themselves started running tasks through free Chinese neural networks. As a result, in early July 2026, Amazon posted a banner on the Mechanical Turk site stating it would stop accepting new clients, marking the end of a mini-era. Even more ironic is that the platform operated for 21 years under the unofficial slogan "Artificial Artificial Intelligence." And, apparently, the time has come for yet another level of abstraction.

Read more

item.title: How to teach any team to solve work tasks with AI
item.description:
Hello everyone, this is Maxim Mikhailov again. In the third article of my series, I talked about why agentic scenarios should not be centrally written by developers alone. AI truly benefits engineers and other specialists when they have a safe environment, accessible tools, and the ability to solve work tasks independently. This is the approach we are developing at our company.

Today, I’ll talk about how to make working with AI a common practice for the entire team.
